summary: Dihydralazine is a direct-acting arteriolar vasodilator of the hydrazinophthalazine class, closely related to hydralazine, used for hypertension and particularly for severe hypertension in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (often given intravenously). It is NOT FDA-approved (hydralazine is the agent marketed in the US); this record is based on European/SmPC, BNF and WHO-type information rather than a US label. It relaxes arteriolar smooth muscle, reducing peripheral vascular resistance and blood pressure, but provokes reflex sympathetic activation (tachycardia, increased cardiac output) and sodium/water retention, so it is often combined with a beta-blocker and a diuretic for chronic use. Like hydralazine, prolonged or high-dose therapy can cause a drug-induced lupus-like syndrome, and it has been linked to immune-mediated hepatitis. Oral dosing is typically around 25 mg two to four times daily; for hypertensive emergencies or pre-eclampsia, small intravenous boluses (about 6.25-12.5 mg) are given slowly with close blood-pressure and fetal monitoring.

moa: Dihydralazine is a direct-acting vasodilator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle predominantly in arterioles, with little effect on veins. By lowering peripheral vascular resistance it reduces arterial blood pressure and afterload. The fall in pressure triggers baroreceptor-mediated reflex sympathetic activation, producing tachycardia and an increase in cardiac output and plasma renin activity, with consequent sodium and water retention. The precise molecular mechanism is thought to involve interference with calcium handling/release in arteriolar smooth muscle; it is metabolised largely by hepatic acetylation, so slow acetylators experience higher exposure and a greater risk of lupus-like reactions.

preg: Dihydralazine (like hydralazine) is used intravenously to control severe hypertension in pregnancy, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, where its benefit is generally considered to outweigh risks; abrupt large falls in blood pressure must be avoided to preserve placental perfusion. Fetal heart-rate monitoring is advised. Neonatal thrombocytopenia has rarely been reported.
lact: Dihydralazine is excreted into breast milk in small amounts. It may be used with caution during breastfeeding while monitoring the infant; many sources consider hydralazine-class drugs compatible at usual doses.
renal: Dihydralazine and its metabolites are partly renally eliminated; in renal impairment, reduce the dose and monitor blood pressure and for accumulation. Hypertension in renal disease may still respond well, but titrate cautiously.
hepatic: Dihydralazine is metabolised hepatically (acetylation). Use cautiously in hepatic impairment; immune-mediated/idiosyncratic hepatitis has been reported with the hydralazine class, so monitor liver function and discontinue if hepatitis is suspected.

pearls: NOT FDA-approved (hydralazine is the US agent) - this record is from EU/SmPC, BNF and WHO-type sources
Direct arteriolar vasodilator - a recognised option for severe hypertension in pregnancy / pre-eclampsia (IV)
Causes reflex tachycardia and fluid retention - combine with a beta-blocker and diuretic for chronic use
Drug-induced lupus-like syndrome with prolonged/high-dose use, more likely in slow acetylators
Immune-mediated hepatitis has been reported - monitor liver function
Avoid abrupt large falls in blood pressure, especially in pregnancy (placental perfusion) and coronary disease
missed: If you miss an oral dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it - do not double up. Keep doses evenly spaced and do not stop the medicine abruptly without advice.
overdose: Overdose causes severe hypotension, marked tachycardia, headache, flushing, myocardial ischaemia and shock. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive: lay the patient flat with legs raised, give intravenous fluids, support blood pressure (vasopressors if needed), and control tachycardia/arrhythmia and myocardial ischaemia; monitor cardiac function continuously.
